EL PASO—Federal Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction Friday to halt construction on the border wall in Texas’ expansive Big Bend sector, including the national and state parks.
Cardone read a brief order from the bench after hearing more than four hours of testimony from conservation groups and residents of the Big Bend region, known internationally for its dark night skies, abundant biodiversity and rugged river canyons.
Cardone said that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits in at least one of their claims and to suffer irreparable harm if construction continues. Her ruling stops border barrier construction in the entire Big Bend sector—which spans more than 500 miles across West Texas—until the federal government complies with all applicable laws.
The ruling applies to all of Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park and the border along the Rio Grande in the rest of the sector. The injunction will remain in place while the court considers the lawsuit, which was filed in April.
Plaintiffs and their supporters embraced and wept outside the federal courtroom in El Paso Friday afternoon following the ruling. Many had traveled hundreds of miles from Big Bend communities, including Terlingua and Marfa, to attend.
The Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and Danny Miller Jr., a river guide, sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin for waiving dozens of laws to fast-track the border wall through the Big Bend region. The Texas Civil Rights Project and the Center for Biological Diversity are representing the plaintiffs.
The federal waivers cover the entire Big Bend region. This had allowed construction to proceed without following the National Environmental Policy Act, the Archaeological and Historic Preservation Act and many other laws. Under the injunction, the effect of the waivers is stayed.
Customs and Border Protection has changed its plans for border barrier construction in the Big Bend region numerous times since February. The federal government currently plans to build vehicle barriers and access roads within the state and national parks. A 30-foot steel wall is planned for private land in Big Bend outside the parks.
In mid-August, advocates documented excavators and bulldozers clearing land within Big Bend National Park. Customs and Border Protection then issued a construction pause in the park on Aug. 17. That pause lifted this week. Construction recently began on a new 30-foot steel wall in Hudspeth County, east of El Paso.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs called eight people to testify Friday. Their arguments centered on the lack of evidence that the Big Bend sector is an area of “high illegal entry,” as stated in the federal waivers. They argued that the plaintiffs were already suffering and will continue to suffer harm if border wall construction continues.
Adam Isaacson, an analyst at the Washington Office on Latin America, presented data showing the Big Bend sector is a “distant last place” in unauthorized border crossings compared to the nine sectors that make up the U.S. border with Mexico. The plaintiffs’ attorneys explained that they requested granular data about how many people are detained in Big Bend National Park, as opposed to the vast area that makes up the rest of the sector, and the federal government never supplied that information.
Miller, the river guide, said his business depends on access to the Rio Grande and explained how property he owns along the river will be irrevocably damaged if the wall is built.
He described border wall construction as a “visible scar that will never go away.” Miller and several other individuals giving testimony broke down in tears when asked how a border wall could change their relationship to the Rio Grande.
U.S. Department of Justice attorneys presented few counterarguments and did not present any witnesses. The White House referred questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.”

"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

The lawyer for the woman who alleges she was raped at a Cornell University fraternity house says she is "not doing well" as she finds herself "under siege" from online sleuths seeking to identity her.
Thomas Giuffra said the woman known in legal documents as Jane Doe was "incapable of consent" because she was "completely, grossly intoxicated" when she turned up at the home where she says the assault took place.
The woman alleges she was raped by seven men at the campus in Ithaca, New York, in 2024.
No charges were initially filed in the case. It has reopened since she filed a civil lawsuit that thrust the claims into the national spotlight, reigniting the possibility of criminal charges.
In an interview on Friday with CNN, Giuffra said: "She's under siege on social media where people are trying to identify her."
He said that postings have "incorrectly" identified other woman as Doe.
In an interview with CBS, the BBC's US partner, Giuffra argued that his client, aged 20 at the time, was unable to provide consent because she was intoxicated when she arrived at the fraternity house.
Giuffra said she had been pressured into taking the drug ketamine before she was allegedly raped.
His comments came as New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state's top prosecutor, Attorney General Letitia James, to take over the investigation.
At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she had "lost faith" in the county prosecutor's ability to oversee the case.
"This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.
She also vowed to close a "loophole" of state law that makes it difficult to press rape charges if an alleged victim voluntarily consumes alcohol or drugs.
Social media feeds are filled with women trying to shield the Cornell accuser's identity by posting videos of themselves under the title "I am Jane Doe".
As well as seeking to complicate internet searches for her name, the messages of solidarity included clips of women detailing their own experiences of sexual assault.
Efforts to rally round Jane Doe gathered pace after a political commentator vowed to unmask her, arguing it was unfair for her to remain anonymous while the men are publicly named despite not being charged with a crime.
Online sleuths have also tried to locate the addresses of the so-called Cornell Seven, leading to at least one case of mistaken identity.
An active-duty US Marine Corps sergeant who had the same name as one of the men was incorrectly served the woman's lawsuit, leading to a torrent of abuse and threats, according to the Free Press, external.

65badfb593e2.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fbi-gives-employees-a-classified-patel-report-about-times-the-agency-fell-short Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI gives employees a classified 'Patel Report' about times the agency 'fell short' Politics Oct 2, 2026 7:46 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI has released a classified report to its workforce examining what it says are chapters from the bureau's history "where this institution fell short," according to an internal message obtained Friday by The Associated Press. It was unclear what episodes from the FBI's past are chronicled in the new "Patel Report." But the document's existence is in keeping with Director Kash Patel's vocal criticism of the leaders who preceded him and with his determination to rid the FBI of agents he contends have politicized the bureau in the past. Patel's critics say he is the one who has weaponized the FBI and that his scrutiny of his predecessors and their decision-making is part of an effort to rewrite history in favor of President Donald Trump. READ MORE: 3 FBI agents fired over Trump investigation get broad backing in lawsuit against administration Patel pledged at his confirmation hearing last year that he would not look "backward," but as director, he has encouraged investigations of former senior officials and presided over sweeping terminations, including of employees who participated in years-old investigations of Trump, were photographed taking a knee during a 2020 racial justice protest and contributed to a disputed analytical memo about Catholic extremism. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The Patel Report looks backward because accountability demands it," says a message to the workforce signed by the FBI's co-deputy directors, Christopher Raia and Andrew Bailey. The message describes the report as marking the "closing of one chapter in our history and the beginning of another complete with a brighter future ahead." Bailey announced his resignation earlier this week, and his last day is Friday. The FBI declined to comment on the report. The message also says: "We cannot change what happened before we arrived. But we can confront it honestly. We can recognize failures instead of protecting them. We can hold people accountable. We can fix what was broken. And we can build safeguards strong enough to ensure the mistakes of the past are never allowed to define this institution again. These steps are consistent with any institution of excellence that is constantly striving for improvement." It was unclear if the report made recommendations or demanded any action to address what the FBI now regards as past shortcomings. The FBI message says the report is meant to "promote fierce organizational accountability" and rebuild "public trust." But Patel's critics say the politically charged investigations into perceived adversaries of Trump that the FBI has embarked on under his watch, as well as the punishment of agents who participated in investigations into the Republican president to which they were assigned, have eroded faith in the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency. For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.
The eerily quiet season continues and with just two months left, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all.
This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.
The biggest reason for this is El NiÃ±o, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.
The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.
With a very strong El NiÃ±o forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.
September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.
But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.
There were, however, four named tropical storms which formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.
All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic.
The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least.
Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El NiÃ±o is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks.
As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible.
In the historical Atlantic hurricane database, there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed.
How does El NiÃ±o affect tropical development?
While El NiÃ±o is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.
As wind patterns shift during an El NiÃ±o, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.
Increased wind shear rips apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.
Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El NiÃ±o because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns.
The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes.
This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.
There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major.
In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point.
El NiÃ±o is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December.

72b09bf024b3.text: By — Mark Lewis, Associated Press Mark Lewis, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/could-the-international-space-station-win-a-nobel-peace-prize-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Could the International Space Station win a Nobel Peace Prize? Here's what to know Science Oct 2, 2026 7:36 PM EDT STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — Not-so-outlandish, prognosticators say: The Nobel Peace Prize this year could go galactic, with an award to the International Space Station. But terrestrial contenders loom too, including U.S. President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, emergency teams in Sudan, children's advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts, experts say. READ MORE: International Space Station marks 25 years of nonstop human presence in orbit The annual guessing game about who will win the prize, often called the most prestigious award on the planet, is revving up ahead of the Norwegian Nobel Committee's Oct. 9 announcement of the winner in Oslo. Predicting the outcome is inherently speculative. Some surprising and controversial choices have appeared over the years. The committee received 287 candidates for this year's prize, and just over a quarter of them are organizations. Experts say the committee, in its process of awarding the prize, typically focuses on the durability of peace, the promotion of international fraternity and the quiet work of institutions that strengthen those goals. International Space Station a symbol of global cooperation Haakon Gjerløw, director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, is considered a top forecaster. He says the ISS — well, the organization behind it — is a rare symbol of global cooperation in a quest toward the heavens at a time when multilateralism is crumbling and many countries have retreated into narrower national interests on Earth. The institute's annual watch list is one of the sources that most informs pundits and punters about the top contenders. Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize, and has been nominated again, but could be viewed as a controversial choice after the U.S., along with Israel, launched an ongoing war on Iran in February. Trump and Canada's Carney are both candidates Canada's Carney has made a mark internationally this year, in large part by standing up to Trump on issues like U.S. tariffs. Gjerløw's list this year also features Ukrainian children's advocate Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children; Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a grassroots relief network; and the Committee to Protect Journalists after the deadliest two years for reporters since record-keeping began nearly 45 years ago. The International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court, jointly, also got a nod. The ICC has faced criticism and controversy among some, and respect from others, over its arrest warrants against leaders like Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump has long criticized the ICC, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to "dismantle the threat … posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty." Later that month, the ICC's chief prosecutor was removed from office over sexual misconduct allegations. Gjerløw said the committee's choice is complicated by recent turmoil after 2025 laureate María Corina Machado of Venezuela, in a symbolic gesture, presented her prize to Trump days after U.S. forces removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power. Conflicts and wars mark this year's prize This year's peace prize comes in an era marked by the most war and conflict in decades, including in Sudan, Ukraine, Yemen, Iran and the Middle East. Shawn Davies, a senior analyst at the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, which monitors conflicts, cited "increased international tensions and changes in the global security order" that he linked to an erosion of U.S. willingness to enforce international rules. Washington has gone from guarantor of the postwar order to a violator of it in some cases, he said. "I don't even think his own base would believe" Trump could win the prize now, "given how he's stuck in what looks like a forever war in Iran," Davies said. Jody Williams, who won the 1997 Peace Prize jointly with the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, says she hopes for a continued trend toward awarding the prize to women. Only 20 of the prize's 112 individual laureates have been women in its 125-year history. In the past 15 years, eight women have won the prize individually, compared to just six men. Among names of the women circulating in prediction markets this year are Gaza surgeon Sara al-Saqqa and Yulia Navalnaya, the Russian opposition figure and widow of Alexei Navalny. Nobels start with prize for medicine Nobel week kicks off Monday with the announcement of the medicine prize, followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization. When it comes to the peace prize selection, expect political fallout no matter who wins. "Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," said Nelson Wiseman, a University of Toronto professor emeritus. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are." The operator of a popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest has been handing out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.
Some videos showing women on the Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, have been viewed millions of times. One is said to have made thousands of euros for a woman who posted it online.
The Teufelsrad is one of the oldest attractions at the Oktoberfest, the annual beer festival which comes to an end this weekend after 16 days. Its circular platform rotates faster and faster until its riders fall off, and the motion and speed often make skirts fly up.
Filming under skirts is illegal in Germany, and carries a two-year sentence in jail.
However, critics believe the law does not go far enough, and the videos of women on the Teufelsrad in their traditional dirndl dresses often show their underwear. Sometimes, the images have been digitally altered to show them naked, according to local broadcaster BR.
One woman made â¬9,000 (Â£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.
At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have been in circulation, according to Munich-based daily SÃ¼ddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been viewed millions of times.
The operator of the Teufelsrad, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC that, for the past three years, she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses, to protect them from people filming in the crowd.
This Oktoberfest she has handed out more than 100 pairs, she says: "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."
Polaczy, who is now 80, said donating cycling shorts wasn't cheap, but it was worth it for her own peace of mind.
The Teufelsrad tent is hung with signs and police posters in German and English warning against filming under people's skirts, but Polaczy says it is impossible to control everyone filming with smart phones.
Some waitresses at this year's beer festival say they have also started wearing cycling shorts under their dirndls.
A spokesman for the Bavarian police told the BBC that since 2025, it has run a poster campaign at the Oktoberfest, warning against upskirting.
This year, police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. Last year there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.
However, Josephine Ballon, who heads German non-profit organisation Hate Aid, which aims to support victims of digital violence, told the BBC that the current law against upskirting does not provide enough protection.
Although she says there are plans for a new law, current legislation "applies only when you film under the skirt", and not when a skirt simply flies up and gets photographed.
The new camera glasses are also a threat, she believes.
Ballon wants anyone who has uploaded intimate pictures of women on the internet to be punished, along with the platforms that put them up.
Meanwhile, the city of Munich has sought to tighten up on influencers and content creators who earn money from their social media postings and who want to film at the Oktoberfest.
Munich has banned broadcasting live streams from the festival and requires anyone who wants to film there to hold a permit, which is issued by the city for a fee.
Hundreds of licences have been issued this year to influencers, who make money from product placement or sponsoring.

An Arizona road rage killer will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video message from his dead victim was improperly aired in court.
Gabriel Paul Horcasitas was found guilty by a jury of shooting and killing Christopher Pelkey, 37, during a confrontation at a red light in 2021. He was sentenced to 10 years behind bars.
But his legal team appealed, arguing that the trial judge should not have allowed an AI video, created by Pelkey's family, to be shown in court ahead of last year's sentencing.
The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, ruling that Horcasitas, 55, must be resentenced because the AI clip "crossed that line".
"Rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the court of appeals wrote on Wednesday.
Horcasitas' lawyer, Kristen Reller, who filed the appeal, declined to comment.
Jessica Gattuso, an attorney for victims in the case, did not respond to a request for comment.
Pelkey's sister, Stacey Wales, told the BBC last year the family had used voice recordings, videos and pictures to recreate him for the AI video.
"To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances," said the AI version of Pelkey in court in 2025. "In another life, we probably could have been friends."
"I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," the AI version of Pelkey - wearing a grey baseball cap - continued.
At the time of the sentencing, the judge who oversaw the case, Todd Lang, seemed to appreciate the use of AI.
"I loved that AI, thank you for that. As angry as you are, as justifiably angry as the family is, I heard the forgiveness," Judge Lang said. "I feel that that was genuine."

Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick â in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it â was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; Â£1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.

Watch: Why students in France are protesting
Protests are continuing across France as students take to the streets to voice their anger over school conditions.
Demonstrations began in the capital Paris nearly two weeks ago and have now escalated and spread to other parts of the country.
More than 500 schools are facing disruption. At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the country's education ministry has said.
The BBC's James Waterhouse is in Paris and witnessed students throwing projectiles and police firing tear gas during clashes.

20fcbd25b9eb.text: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind.

A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko has said, as Russia ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.
The attack on Saturday morning damaged the road surface and trolleybus overhead wires on the Northern Bridge, Klitschko said.
The strike comes after another key bridge in the city, Southern Bridge, has been targeted multiple times by Russian drones since Thursday, with Klitschko earlier warning that such attacks were "tearing Kyiv apart".
The two bridges link the eastern and western parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday, signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks.
Writing on Telegram on Saturday, Klitschko said: "Hitting the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way."
"Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added.
Earlier attacks on the Southern Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Following the meeting, Klitschko said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.
After the Southern Bridge was attacked on Thursday, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.
Metro trains were suspended but road traffic was eventually allowed to resume.
Similar disruption continued on Friday following further strikes.

Environmental experts, conservation groups and businesses from across the British Isles and France have gathered in Guernsey for the 26th Inter-Island Environment Meeting.
The annual event, co-ordinated by the Guernsey Nature Commission, brings together delegates to share ideas and develop joint projects aimed at protecting the natural environment.
This year's theme, Nature for the Next Generation, includes talks on subjects ranging from seabird restoration and woodland resilience to butterfly monitoring in Sark and citizen science projects.
A Sixth Form Environment Meeting gave young people the chance to present environmental issues that matter to them and contribute ideas for the future.
'Share successes'
Students will take part in workshops linked to Guernsey's upcoming Marine Spatial Plan, helping shape discussions about the future protection and management of the island's seas.
Angela Salmon, head of education at the Nature Commission and a member of the meeting group said inviting sixth formers to share the environmental issues that mattered to them "makes perfect sense".
Among those attending was Sebastian Dufour, an independent consultant for the Alderney Wildlife Trust, who joined a field trip to Lihou Island exploring its ecology and archaeology.
He said he had learned about a Benedictine Priory site "which is very interesting" and discovered there had been "a really remarkably large industry in harvesting seaweed".
Dufour said he particularly valued the collaborative nature of the event, adding: "We're all coming from different islands and we're all facing similar challenges."
He said the annual meeting provided an opportunity to "learn from each other" and "share our successes and failures and everything".

The co-pilot of the Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe in an attempt to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged some 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and take control of the plane.
Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.
Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.
A crash axe is usually kept âin the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that, after being subdued, the attacker called out to the crew, "Kill me, kill me!"
He added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidalâ¦ It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
The pilot, from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.
About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply.
The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.
In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.
Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."
People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit.
Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries.
Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".
Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.
Zvika Manes told Israeli public broadcaster Kan that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

After years trudging through marshes around San Francisco Bay studying conservation practices, coastal ecologist Megan Kelso realized that one of the largest determinants of wetland health may not be an invasive species lurking with her among the sea grasses, but decisions made miles away in the executive suites of insurance companies.
Wetlands absorb massive volumes of carbon and are vital to combating climate change, Kelso said, and she saw her early field work as the most effective way to keep them healthy.
It wasn’t until she started working alongside Mike Beck, director of University of California Santa Cruz’s coastal resilience program, and was offered a grant to research how insurance can promote similar habitat restoration projects, that she had her “aha” moment.
“I was thinking, maybe there’s a way to align this huge sector of insurance with nature and conservation in a way that could have a bigger impact than what I was doing before,” Kelso said.
Now her research is the basis of a new study published in the science journal Nature by Kelso and five co-authors that outlines what these “nature-based” insurance policies would look like and how they could benefit both insurance companies and policyholders in the long run.
“It could be tens of billions of dollars going towards nature-based projects that reduce your risk,” Kelso told Inside Climate News. “It’s this big lever that hasn’t really been fully utilized yet.”
One set of policies are those designed to insure nature, such as a policy backed by insurance giant Swiss Re that provides payouts to local Mexican governments and businesses on the Yucatán peninsula when storms damage nearby coral reefs off the peninsula’s coast.
The other set, sometimes called resilience insurance, reduces policyholders’ premiums for mitigating the likelihood or severity of damage their property would incur from natural risks like wildfire, by using prescribed burns to sustainably manage surrounding forest, installing ember-resistant vents in buildings, or managing flooding by cultivating wetlands.
There are already models capable of calculating the cost savings natural features provide when calamity strikes, according to Kelso—one study found that salt marshes blunted Superstorm Sandy’s damages by 15 percent, and another estimated that natural fire buffers would have cut the financial toll of California’s 2018 Paradise Fire by 21 percent.
Instead of recreating those models, Kelso’s paper serves as a playbook illustrating how the insurance industry can incorporate risk reduction estimates into future policies, pass those savings on to consumers and fund new hazard mitigation projects, all at a profit.
“Your average person working in the insurance industry may think that it’s a small impact, but it can be very large in some circumstances, like 15 to 25 percent risk reduction from intact habitats,” Kelso said.
Nature-Based Insurance in Action
As insurance premiums across the U.S. continue to climb and wildfires engulf the Pacific Northwest, the promise of a solution that mitigates both in the face of climate change is especially significant.
Former California state Insurance Commissioner Dave Jones came to this realization nearly a decade ago when home insurance non-renewals began climbing after especially costly wildfires in 2016 and 2017.
Jones had addressed his initial climate concerns a couple years prior with policies that require insurance companies in California to disclose their investments in fossil fuel industries, but as non-renewals spiked, he convened home insurers once more and requested they voluntarily make significant investments in scientific research on wildfire risk mitigation.
“They looked at me like I was from Mars,” Jones recalled, adding that the insurance executives told him, “‘We’re not arguing with the science… but we’re in the risk transfer business, not the risk mitigation business.’”
“Sadly, that has continued to be the case,” Jones said.
After he left office in 2019, Jones set out to contribute to wildfire risk mitigation research with The Nature Conservancy.
His first contribution was a groundbreaking 2021 study from TNC and multinational insurance broker Willis Towers Watson that projected forestry practices like prescribed fire and understory thinning had the potential to lower homeowner premiums in a northern California community by 20 to 40 percent, primarily by reducing the frequency and severity of potential wildfire.
The model was then adapted in 2025 to create a nascent wildfire resilience insurance policy for a 25,000-member homeowner association near Truckee, Calif. The model rewarded the Tahoe Donner Association’s historic wildfire mitigation efforts with a 39 percent lower premium price and 84 percent lower deductible for a policy covering over 1,000 acres of forest and recreation land.
“This is a geography where other insurers are declining to write or renew” insurance policies, Jones said. “It was an important demonstration that insurers can take landscape-scale, nature-based insurance into account and write insurance accordingly.”
To Kelso, the policy is proof that resilience insurance is feasible in real life and at a broad scale. The policy allows for the HOA to funnel its premium savings back into the forestry practices that initially earned it the discount and perpetually fund those practices into the future.
“The property insurance market is so huge that even if some small percentage of the money that goes into paying for premiums could be diverted towards reducing your risk… could be a game changer for conservation and restoration,” Kelso said.
A year later and a separate HOA down the Sierra Nevada mountain range closer to Lake Tahoe is working to adopt a similar policy, according to Jones.
He and Kelso are in agreement that the success of these insurance models is reliant on widespread customer demand and adoption. Absent that, insurers and risk modelers won’t be incentivised to gather data or fine-t

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission wants to scrap a rule that allows shareholders to formally petition companies, one of the ways that shareholder advocacy groups have pressed for more action on climate and sustainability.
Investor and advocacy groups warn that the SEC’s move would block a longstanding avenue for pressuring public companies to factor in climate risks that could severely impact their operations.
For instance, investors have used the rule to persuade companies to be more transparent on their emission targets and to better account for other environmental impacts. In 2022, nearly two-thirds of Home Depot shareholders backed a proposal on deforestation in its supply chains. Home Depot commissioned a third-party assessment and released a report in 2024.
“Taking away the right of shareholders to petition companies about climate change really is taking away another tool … not only from investors, but also from the public, to address the climate issue,” said Timothy Smith, senior policy advisor at the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, a coalition of faith- and values-based investors.
During the 2026 season for companies’ annual shareholder meetings, ICCR members filed 438 shareholder proposals. Fifty were related to the climate crisis, and half of these were brought up for a vote before all shareholders. Smith said scrapping the existing rules will not only remove shareholders’ right to petition companies but will also create a void for the companies by dismantling the structured pathway they had for shareholder engagement.
The SEC introduced the current rules in 1942, allowing eligible investors to submit proposals to public companies for a vote at the annual shareholder meeting. The proposals are simply recommendations, but companies may feel more pressure to act when they get a lot of shareholder support.
Most companies rarely see shareholder proposals. The Council of Institutional Investors—a nonprofit association of U.S. asset owners and managers—looked at companies in an index representing most publicly traded firms in the U.S., and found an average of one shareholder proposal per company every 7.7 years.
But some large oil and gas firms are among those receiving far more than average. The American Petroleum Institute has pushed for years to change shareholder-proposal rules. ExxonMobil sued to block a climate proposal related to its greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, citing “micromanagement”; the case was dismissed after the shareholder agreed not to submit any more climate-related proposals.
Climate risks are “very topical and very critical” for investors with the increased use of artificial intelligence, said Bryan McGannon, managing director of the Sustainable Investment Forum, an investor group based in the U.S. Investors need to understand how companies are employing AI and how that affects their energy and water usage, he said.
The SEC argues that its move hands power to states. An SEC spokesperson said in a statement that the agency’s proposal would provide states with both the legal clarity and the motivation to implement their own ideas for a “sensible shareholder proposal framework.” The spokesperson added that the changes would take companies’ focus off “debates that have little or no bearing on investors’ financial returns.”
But the Trump administration has, across agencies, sought to reduce checks on corporate behavior—rolling back protections against everything from pollution to financial meltdowns. Other proposals from the SEC include halving the number of times companies must report their earnings and letting most of them avoid financial scrutiny from outside auditors.
The SEC’s new proposal, published in the Federal Register last week, came after the agency removed itself from a key part of the shareholder-petition process. Earlier, if a company thought a shareholder proposal didn’t meet the requirements to be brought up for a vote among all shareholders, it could ask the agency to weigh in. The SEC sharply limited its involvement in this “no-action” process late last year and stopped completely in August.
McGannon says this “dramatically lowered” the number of shareholder proposals in the past year, including those on environmental issues. He fears the SEC’s new rule changes would further reduce the number.
Investor groups say it’s not yet clear how shareholder proposals would work once the rule change is in place. States have no such regulations yet, Smith said.
While shareholders could still submit proposals, investor advocates say what happens next would be at the discretion of each company.

Reuters reported last week that Microsoft committed to accepting shareholder proposals through next year.
From 2025 to 2026, shareholder proposals across an index reflecting most of the companies traded in the U.S. fell by approximately 20 percent, according to a report by The Conference Board, a business membership and research group. During the same period, the group found, environmental proposals declined by 32 percent, even as the ones shareholders submitted received slightly more support during voting.
Not all shareholder proposals end up receiving a vote, because in most cases shareholders and businesses discuss the matter and reach middle ground, said Andrew Collier, director of the Freedom to Invest initiative at Ceres, a nonprofit advocacy organization working with institutional investors. That process is critical for companies to protect shareholder value, he said.
“This is a big deal for investors,” he said.
Far from helping companies, Collier said, the Trump administration’s plan would replace “a predictable national system run by the SEC with a patchwork of state rules.”

Asian Games - final round
-18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chi), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe)
Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.
The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes.
There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see.
Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.
However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal-winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.
Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.
Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.
His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption.
Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.
However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.

From our collaborating partner Living on Earth, public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by Jenni Doering with author Craig Childs.
Think about the darkest sky you’ve ever seen. Did you see the Milky Way? Did starlight cast shadows?
This kind of experience is becoming rare in our brightly lit world, but the stars are still out there, waiting for us to rediscover them.
That’s the focus of the 2025 book “The Wild Dark: Finding the Night Sky in the Age of Light,” by naturalist, wilderness explorer and award-winning author Craig Childs, who lives on the remote Colorado Plateau. This interview has been edited for length and clarity; the full interview is available in the audio link above.
JENNI DOERING: What attracts you to the night sky and the stars? And when did you first feel this pull to reflect more on the mysteries above us?
CHILDS: It’s impossible not to be attracted to the night sky. I think everybody is. That was a nice thing about writing this—I thought, “Oh, here’s something that everybody loves, even people who are disconnected from it, who don’t see it.” There’s something intrinsic about looking up and seeing a sky full of stars. Something I wrote about in the book was when I was five years old, I was camping out in the woods with my mom and her boyfriend, and they took off into the night and left me on this mattress. They’d carried a full mattress out into the woods, and I was under all these blankets, and I was terrified of the dark. But then I saw the stars, and I remember that. I remember how clear they were, and how much it calmed me down to look up and see, really to see infinity for the first time, or at least to recognize it for the first time … there was something just deeply calming about it. To know that there was infinity that you could see forever, and it wasn’t empty. It was full.
DOERING: In this book, “The Wild Dark,” we follow you on this journey from one of the brightest places on Earth, Las Vegas, to one of the darkest. Why did you and your companion Irvin choose to bike through the desert to take on this quest? And what questions did you want to ponder while you were on this trip?
CHILDS: A bike made sense—human-powered speed—because driving out of Las Vegas, if you wanted to get to the darkest of the dark, you’d be there in three hours. I was much more interested in the transition, in letting my eyes adjust and seeing what the different nights are like.
That took us about 200 miles through the backcountry on fully loaded mountain bikes, self-supported. We were going maybe 20 miles a day, and that was enough to make every night significantly different for nine nights. The question I had was: What are each of these skies like? Not just the darkest, not just the brightest, but the ones in between. And how different are they?
DOERING: You picked nine days and nine nights because there are nine different levels on the Bortle scale, which we use to delineate the quality of the skies at night. What is the Bortle scale for people who haven’t heard of this funny-sounding thing?
CHILDS: I love the word “Bortle” because it sounds like it should be a space word, but it’s actually somebody’s name. John E. Bortle is an amateur astronomer who identifies comets, and he needed a way to express the night sky in non-technical terms, in naked-eye terms. He came up with the nine levels, Bortle One being the darkest, and Bortle Nine being that lemony sky over Las Vegas … We were still getting shadows from Vegas 170 miles out.
DOERING: The climate crisis is rapidly changing our world, but what about what’s happening with light? How fast is artificial light expanding, and how is it reshaping the way we live?
CHILDS: Writing this book, I hesitated to say, “Oh, here’s another problem.” Like, add this to your load. Except, it’s a different kind of problem than climate change or heavy metals in a river. These are all long-term generational difficulties that take a lot of thinking, whereas light is something where you turn off the switch, and the night sky is there immediately.
But the Earth has never had this much light in its history. It changes our circadian rhythms, changes how we relate to the world and it takes away the night sky.
When the LED boom came in the late ’90s, early 2000s, lighting around the world increased dramatically, but I have talked to some lighting engineers who say that they think we are over the hump of peak lighting, that we’re actually going to be changing in decades to come, where we understand light more, we understand how to place it more, we understand that it doesn’t need to be everywhere, and it doesn’t need to be lighting up the skies. And we don’t need it to be safe, as in we don’t need it to be blinding to be safe. We need it to be strategic. They’re seeing the possibility that the world might actually darken, that nights might go back to the stars, and that’s a future that I really am interested in because this is a problem we can solve very easily.
DOERING: What relationship does wildlife have to the night sky? To what extent are animals and plants being affected by this currently bright planet?
CHILDS: In a big way, it’s navigation. When I was looking at Las Vegas, I was looking at these swarms of grasshoppers, millions upon millions of grasshoppers that sweep into the city at certain times. They’re drawn from the surrounding desert to the light. Animals are drawn to light, and birds are drawn to stationary light. Birds that are navigating spring and fall pay attention to where Polaris, the North Star, sits, because it’s the one star that doesn’t move, and that defines their north-south migrations. When you have cities sitting along their major flyways, you have all these stationary lights, and they are pulled toward them.
I was down at the memorial lights for Ground Zero in Manhattan the year after the [Twin Towers] fell. What I noticed when I got down right beneath them, looking up, was that they were full of thousands and thous

Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek.
Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain.
The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint.
On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title.
"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport.
"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality."
Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China.
She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter.
Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent.
Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury.
"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong.
Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title.
Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way.
"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong.
"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense."
The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025.
The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023.
Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China.
If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili.
"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong.
The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira.
When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response.
"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.
Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.
Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?
Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.
It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.
'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.
On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.
Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.
Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.
But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.
What could cause it?
Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.
Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.
Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.
Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration.
"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.
This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".
Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.
Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.
She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself.
Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, Hac says. Women and children are more susceptible, experts say.
Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.
