Investigators in the US state of Georgia are on the hunt for a suspect in a mass shooting that erupted in the early hours of Sunday, killing two people and injuring 35 more.
A crowd of roughly 1,000 people had gathered for a block party in the southern rural community of Vienna when, according to officials, more than 50 shots were fired.
Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while another 25 were transported to multiple nearby hospitals, some in critical condition.
No known arrests have been made and authorities have not given a possible motive for the violence. Victims ranged in age from 14 to 51.
The incident occurred on Sunday morning around 01:30 local time (05:30 GMT), during a Dooly High School homecoming celebration, though it was not a school-sponsored event.
"Our hearts are with the families grieving the loss of loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone affected by this tragedy," the school said in a statement.
Anticipating a large gathering, authorities from the Dooly County Sheriff's Office were already positioned at both ends of the crowd as gunfire rang out.
"Some people were reporting fireworks and then someone said somebody been shot," Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told local media.
Peavy said officials then worked their way through the crowd, as people ran scrambling in different directions, while authorities made their way towards victims.
Ashley Gee, who was there, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution news outlet that the barrage of gunfire sounded "like a machine gun".
Authorities arrived and found several people injured. The two deceased victims were found several blocks away from the scene of the shooting on Pine Street.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigations Medical Examiner's Office said it would conduct an autopsy in each case.
The bureau also said it would join the investigation at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, describing operations as "active and ongoing".

f41d1de48d4c.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/listen-live-supreme-court-hears-case-seeking-damages-from-fossil-fuel-industry-for-climate-change Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LISTEN LIVE: Supreme Court hears case seeking damages from fossil fuel industry for climate change Politics Oct 5, 2026 7:50 AM EDT LOUISVILLE, Colo. (AP) — Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo's Colorado home was in ashes. Supreme Court arguments are expected to begin at 10 a.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough. READ MORE: Supreme Court ready to tackle climate, immigration and gun rights. Here are 5 cases to watch "We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again," Somauroo said. "At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change. The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court's new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it. The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters. The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue. READ MORE: Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants "The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth," said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers' Accountability Project, an industry group. "We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn't do that." The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab. "No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large," they wrote. The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations. Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument. WATCH: What the Supreme Court's voter-citizenship database decision means for the midterms Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs. "Boulder County and city aren't trying to change what's happening in Texas or New York, they're trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado," said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case. Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo's home, after the county's suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history. "Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent," said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado. WATCH: What Trump's rollback of fuel economy standards means for drivers The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants. Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it's unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential "off-ramp": whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage. Whitehurst reported from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press

The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.
The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.
He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.
Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".
More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight â whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami â emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.
Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.
He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX â with more than 180 passengers on board â into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.
The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.
The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.
There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.
But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.
Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".
Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?
Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful".
The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene.
BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best".
"It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse.
But they do tell a story.
Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager.
His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak.
Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing.
Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives, external and is personal to them.
His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify.
According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple.
When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song.
"I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says.
"For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this."
Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists.
He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry.
Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space".
"We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says.
Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success.
Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently.
But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon".
"They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says.
"It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out."
The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out.
"There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet.
"When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it."
Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages , externalof Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram.
There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years.
Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way".
"The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says.
But, he adds: "I'm not there yet".
However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart.
"He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain.
"Maybe the universe will just make it happen."

The Premier League panel's report laid it out in black and white.
"The club's income was hugely overstated by over Â£830 million."
In other words, Manchester City's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations over a number of years by pumping money into the club that should not have been recorded as sponsorship income.
The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.
Contained within it was an interest payment of Â£37m, an increase from Â£34m the previous year.
And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of Â£852m.
Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city resulted in money being ploughed in, it meant a similar significant sum being paid out in interest for the other.
Maintaining financial discipline
United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."
This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.
Record revenues of Â£677.6m, projected to go as high as Â£760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.
Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.
In confirming they had spent Â£191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional Â£90m. It took their overall debt to Â£1.15bn.
To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was Â£667m.
Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was Â£375m. Of that, Â£218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another Â£122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets â although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.
When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (Â£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said Â£63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.
Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.
Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.
In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at Â£313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to Â£302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.
While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.
Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer â their Â£148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others â their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.
When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated Â£47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.
Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for Â£74m in 2019, United have only generated more than Â£25m for a player on four occasions â for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.
It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.
In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.
Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.
The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.
Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium â all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.
In 2017-18, United made Â£80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got Â£31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a Â£10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.

Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (Â£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals â affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations â areas where India still falls short.
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.

US convicted murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear days after Tennessee authorities botched her execution by lethal injection, her lawyer said.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, raised a number of questions, including what went wrong? And what happens next?
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who has halted executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. The head of prisons in the state is also resigning after the failed execution.
How did it go wrong?
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the 11th hour.
She was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital, but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat. As of Thursday night, she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator.
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion on Friday to preserve "any and all evidence" related to her botched execution.
During the execution attempt, prison officials tried to start intravenous (IV) lines by using at least seven needles on Pike, according to her lawyers.
While receiving the two doses, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly", her lawyers said.
"At no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body," her lawyers said in the filing.
Her lawyers had warned something like this might occur.
In January, Pike's legal team filed a lawsuit, external challenging the state's lethal injection protocol. In it, they said Pike suffered from a blood-clotting condition known as thrombocytosis and said she had "small veins that make insertion of a needle more difficult".
After the botched execution, Pike's attorney Stephen Ferrell said setting an IV line was more difficult than a simple blood draw, adding: "We knew this was coming."
Pike's other attorney, Randy Spivey, said he noticed during the execution that "her right arm was turning purple" and that there was "burning around the sites of the injection" afterwards.
Pike's lawyers also raised the issue of degraded pentobarbital, suggesting that it may have lost its potency.
On Sunday, while speaking to CNN, Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not explained why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal.
On Saturday, Tennessee Governor Lee announced the state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada was stepping down. Lee said it was "in the best interests" of the state and called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary".
Opponents of the death penalty said it was difficult to know what went wrong, because part of Pike's execution happened behind a curtain.
Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "Lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
How did she survive?
Pike survived two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbital. Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said this was enough that, had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation, "she would have surely died".
Zivot said the only possible explanation for her survival "is that the pentobarbital blood level was never high enough to cause death" and that blisters on her arm after the botched execution indicated a ruptured vein.
So, instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, he said, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.
Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis may have also played a role, forming blood clots at the injection site that would potentially block pentobarbital from entering her veins.
Regarding the possibility the pentobarbital was degraded, Zivot explained that if this was the case, it could be due to factors including poor manufacturing or improper storage.
What happens next?
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility. Hospital staff were working to save her life and clear the drug used, pentobarbital, from her system, her lawyers said in a court filing on Friday.
Dr Joel Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she [Pike] will have a brain injury."
Pike's lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted, but it is not clear what might happen next.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use

Astronomers may have spotted a fun-sized version of one of the brightest and most mysterious cosmic objects. An elusive microblazar, a scaled-down form of the giant, ravenous black holes that haunt the distant universe, seems to have cropped up in our own Milky Way galaxy.
Even more intriguingly, the exotic object may explain the longstanding mystery of how some of the highest-energy particles in the universe came to be, researchers report in a forthcoming paper in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
Blazars are a particular form of quasars, supermassive black holes whose gravity pulls surrounding material into a whirling disk. In this extreme environment, the quasar flings superheated material out in a pair of jets like the axle of a wheel. A blazar is any quasar that points one of its jets approximately toward Earth.
Astronomers haven’t found quasars or blazars anywhere near Earth, but for nearly 35 years they have hunted for miniature ones in the Milky Way. Such a microquasar consists of a small black hole devouring a large star and sending jets of material spewing out into space. Because they are so much smaller than quasars, material falls into them faster than their massive counterparts.
“What takes days or weeks to change in a microblazar would take thousands of years in a supermassive blazar,” says astrophysicist Pedro Luque-Escamilla of the University of Jaén in Spain. “It’s a perfect scale model where we can watch a ‘cosmic movie’ in fast-forward.”
Luque-Escamilla and his colleague Josep Martí have spent two decades hunting for these hyperactive objects in archival telescope data, with little success. “We found many candidates in the past,” Martí says. “They turned out to be extragalactic objects,” full-sized and slower-changing.
The pair’s luck changed as they pored over a 1983 catalog produced by a Dutch-American spacecraft and spotted an object referred to as IRAS 18293−0941. When Martí and his colleague cross-referenced this catalog with modern observations by radio telescopes, they saw a small but very bright emission with additional light coming from only one side. That’s “the fingerprint of blazars,” Martí says.
The researchers assumed that, like their previous candidates, IRAS 18293−0941 was a full-sized blazar from beyond the Milky Way. But they were intrigued enough to keep investigating. The team ultimately used data from three different observatories on Earth and in space to pinpoint the location as inside our galaxy after all.
“The authors took a truly multi-wavelength approach, making use of all different types of astrophysical data from many telescopes,” says astrophysicist Alexandra Tetarenko of the University of Lethbridge in Canada, who was not involved in the new research. “This is not only what distinguishes this work from past claims on other microblazar candidates but also makes it far more convincing.”
The scientists also noticed that IRAS 18293−0941 was quite near a known patch of ultrahigh energy particles — particles with energy 100 times higher than the Large Hadron Collider can create, that scientists have struggled to explain what could juice them up to such extremes.
Martí and his colleagues argue this isn’t a coincidence: the “hotspot” marks where the microblazar’s invisible jet pointing away from Earth slams into a cloud of matter, acting as a massive particle accelerator. The team is already working to gather additional observations of the proposed hotspot.
The hotspot observations, as well as observations of the visible jet, should both give scientists a better understanding of the microblazar’s dramatic capacities, Luque-Escamilla says, as if the universe made a special particle accelerator just for scientists. “It’s like comparing a high-tech human laboratory to a supreme cosmic engine,” he says.

In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival's many legal woes. Image problems for both candidates While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians' lives. But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals. He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics. He watched the count with friends at a bar. "I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win," he said. Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro's eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps. "I voted for his father, and I don't regret it," she said. The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father's presidency, "people felt more at ease to discriminate," she said. "I'm an LGBTQ+ woman, I can't think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected," she added. Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula's social policies that help the "less fortunate" and how he stands up to Trump. "That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there," she said at a voting center in Brasilia. "He won't succeed if Lula wins." A museum plaque has been unveiled in honour of the scientist who developed the Beagle 2 probe - the first British and European spacecraft to land on another planet.
The tribute, at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises the space probe landing on Mars on Christmas Day 2003 and honours the contribution to the mission of the late Bristol-born scientist Professor Colin Pillinger.
"He was exceptional," said UK Space Agency former chief scientist Chris Lee who worked on Beagle 2 with Pillinger. "He managed to get everybody excited about space exploration."
Another 12 plaques were announced earlier this year to be installed at a number of sites linked to the historic landing.
Lee was one of the Filton space crew who contributed to the Beagle 2 mission before he became a leading scientist for the UK Space Agency.
"We were at the time the principal place for space exploration in the UK and Colin came to us because of our experience," Lee said.
"He was always very positive, one of those can-do figures. Where we would see problems, he would see solutions."
The unveiling of the Beagle 2 plaque, located in the People Gallery at the M Shed, took place on Monday.
Bristol City Council's Head of Culture Philip Walker said they wanted to celebrate the achievements of Pillinger, who grew up in Kingswood, and his team.
"It's great to be able to celebrate his contribution to the city," he said.
Pillinger, who died in 2014, passed away before pictures of the landing site revealed Beagle 2 did not crash-land on Mars as had previously been thought.
But although the landing of Beagle 2 was successful, it was branded as a failed mission as it was unable to connect back to Earth once it landed.
The mission landing is still regarded, however, as an historic success for the European Space Agency which has subsequently influenced future exploration.
In the years that followed the Beagle 2 mission, the UK contributed significantly to flagship space projects, including the Rosetta comet chaser and the James Webb Space Telescope.
"Beagle 2 started the UK down the line of being able to do planetary missions and knowing it could engineer them," said Professor Mark Sims, who managed the Beagle 2 mission.
A more recent example is the ExoMars Rover, Rosalind Franklin, which is due for launch in 2028 with the aim of finding out if life has ever existed on Mars.
"It's a European Space Agency mission but the rover was built in Stevenage and it will land on Mars hopefully in 2030 and look for signs of life which is what Beagle 2 was aiming to do," Sims said.

People are being urged not to bathe at a beach after creosote was identified in a pollution investigation.
In August, members of the public were urged not to swim at Blyth South Beach in Northumberland after reports of "oil like pollution" and a fuel smell.
Laboratory tests confirmed the substance as creosote, with investigations suggesting the cause as an ex-timber treatment works operating on land adjacent to the affected area until about 1980, Northumberland County Council said.
The council, Environment Agency (EA) and Port of Blyth said they were working to respond to the ongoing pollution, and restrictions remain in place on the land between Blyth West Pier and the Dave Stephens Centre.
An EA investigation has found the pollution is contained within an area of the beach near the Hole in the Wall, where it is seeping into the sand through contaminated groundwater.
The council said the public health risk was low, but urged people to keep their dogs away from the affected area of beach and water and to avoid contact themselves.
It is not yet known how long the clean-up will take, but it has been described as a "significant" piece of work.

95972e64d4b0.text: Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican speaker in U.S. history who later admitted sexually abusing several teenage boys, died Saturday at 84. The big picture: Hastert was the highest-ranking elected official in U.S. history to serve time in federal prison, and Congress still conducts business under an unwritten rule bearing his name. Driving the news: Hastert died at his home in Plano, Illinois, while under hospice care, the Kendall County Coroner's Office told Axios in an emailed statement. Catch up quick: Hastert pleaded guilty to evading banking laws in 2015 after prosecutors investigated him for concealing large cash withdrawals. Court proceedings revealed he paid hush money to cover up his past sexual abuse of boys while working as a teacher and high school wrestling coach. Prosecutors alleged that Hastert molested at least four boys, some as young as 14. He faced no sexual abuse charges due to statutes of limitations. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison and released in 2017 after serving 13 months. Zoom out: While in Congress, Hastert became known for the unwritten Hastert Rule, under which the speaker will only bring a bill to the floor for a vote if a majority of the majority party supports it. Critics say the rule encouraged partisanship by keeping bipartisan bills off the floor if they lack support from most members of the majority party. Hastert is survived by his wife, Jean Kahl, and their two sons. Go deeper: Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert settles child sexual abuse payments suit Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Justices declined to hear Moore's appeal of a lower court decision that vacated the large verdict. The outcome keeps in place the decision by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that erased a jury's decision that Moore had been defamed by the ad. READ MORE: Sacha Baron Cohen defeats $95 million defamation suit filed by Roy Moore It was a victory for Senate Majority PAC, which funded the ad, and argued it was truthful. The decision comes months after the court in June rejected Moore's emergency request to put the 11th Circuit decision on hold while he appealed. Moore, a former Alabama chief justice, known for his hardline stances opposing same-sex marriage and supporting the public display of the Ten Commandments, lost the 2017 Senate race after his campaign was rocked by misconduct allegations. Leigh Corfman said Moore inappropriately touched her in 1979 when she was 14 and he was a 32-year-old assistant district attorney. Moore denied the accusation. Other women said Moore dated them, or asked them out on dates, when they were older teens. Senate Majority PAC funded Highway 31, a group that ran an advertising blitz against Moore during the Senate race. Moore filed a defamation lawsuit against Senate Majority PAC centered on a television ad. Moore's attorneys argued the ad juxtaposed statements and partial quotes from separate news articles that, when read together, falsely implied he was accused of soliciting sex from young girls at a shopping mall. Moore's attorneys called it a "fabricated accusation, never made by any reporter" that was "broadcast into Alabama homes 533 times in the final days of a United States Senate election." A federal jury in 2022 agreed with Moore and awarded him $8.2 million in damages. The appeals court vacated the verdict after finding Moore failed to prove the organization acted with malice, one of the legal standards for cases involving public figures. Moore appealed to the Supreme Court. Associated Press writer Lindsay Whitehurst in Washington contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 0d4028a52b96.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-russian-report-says-a-worker-at-a-siberian-plague-research-institute-fell-ill-and-died-of-an-unknown-cause Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A Russian report says a worker at a Siberian plague research institute fell ill and died of an unknown cause World Oct 5, 2026 10:03 AM EDT Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an "unknown" cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week. WATCH: Authors of 'In Covid's Wake' on their criticism of the government's pandemic response Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person. The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk. The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital's outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said. Anna Popova, head of Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday. Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn't identify the infection and called it a suspected case of "a particularly dangerous infection." Rospotrebnadzor was implementing "a full range of anti-epidemic measures," he added. Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology," and said "extensive" testing found "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities." The agency also said it didn't uncover any incidents at the institute "involving pathogenic microorganisms." Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative. Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the woman died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine. Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than "rumors or speculation." The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said Saturday on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: "Better be safe than sorry." The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas. Across the continent, persistent failures in national grids and growing populations have already created an off-grid âshadowâ fuel market, predominantly led by diesel generators. However, the recent rise in fuel prices due to the Iran war, alongside the removal of subsidies in Nigeria and a significant drop in solar panel prices in recent decades, are driving the shift to solar.

Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives.
Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state.
The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping.
Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; Â£28,440), which he could not afford.
"There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.
Adewale appealed to the government for help.
Those kidnapped had been travelling from Ibadan in the south-west to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states on Thursday when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state.
The NYSC is a compulsory one-year programme for most Nigerian university and polytechnic graduates. Participants, known as corps members, are posted to different parts of the country to work and take part in community service, as well as to foster a sense of national unity.
Speaking to journalists, Bosso said they had tracked the kidnappers.
"The drone actually showed us exactly their location. But our predicament is that with the intel we have... the camp is mined with IEDs [homemade bombs]," he said.
Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are being deployed as police prepare for a rescue operation.
Kidnapping for ransom is a major security problem in Nigeria, involving both criminal gangs and armed groups.
The abduction in Imo state has caused widespread concern, with mass kidnappings less common in southern Nigeria than in some parts of the north.
Paying ransoms is illegal and authorities have repeatedly warned families against doing so, but relatives of kidnapped people are often under pressure to do so to secure their release.
The latest abduction highlights the risks faced by young people travelling across Nigeria to do their national youth service and has renewed calls for reforms.
The NYSC has previously said it would not deploy members to areas considered high-risk because of violence or the threat of abduction. Most parts of south-eastern Nigeria have not previously been classified as high-risk areas.
In the south-east, some previous abductions have been linked to separatist groups, including the Indigenous People of Biafra (Ipob).
Authorities have not linked the current abduction to any group.

346add02b75d.text: By — Michael Tarm, Associated Press Michael Tarm, Associated Press By — Herbert G. McCann, Associated Press Herbert G. McCann, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/dennis-hastert-longtime-republican-house-speaker-who-went-to-prison-dies-at-age-84 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84 Politics Oct 5, 2026 11:25 AM EDT CHICAGO (AP) — Dennis Hastert, whose legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84. Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007 and spent more than a year in prison later in life, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison. In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job in 1999, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial. After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda. In 2015 he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors said Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in Yorkville, a small town west of Chicago. Prosecutors said Hastert sexually abused at least four team members during his coaching career, which lasted from 1965 to 1981. The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them. Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered. Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash. At the sentencing hearing, where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." WATCH: Hastert faces sex abuse past in hush money case In a statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse. When he became House speaker, Hastert was aware of the pitfalls of holding the powerful position. "You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground." As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock. "I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," Hastert wrote in a 2004 memoir. Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck. In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold. Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race. In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995. Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district. He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year. Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967. In 2007, Wheaton named its new public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber. Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family's feed business. Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons. Tarm and McCann are former Associated Press reporters. Associated Press reporter Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned a "horrific" Russian attack on a vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea.
The ship's captain was killed in the strike involving two drones, Zelensky said, and another sailor was unaccounted for. Eleven crew members - nationals of Azerbaijan and India - have been rescued.
Romania said it had mounted a rescue mission after "a fire on the ship Royad Mammadov" outside the country's territorial waters. It said two people had died.
Russia has not commented, but its defence ministry earlier said it had struck two cargo vessels. Russia has been pounding Ukrainian infrastructure in what it says is retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and ships in the Black Sea.
Monday's attack by Russia targeted "a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey", Volodymyr Zelensky said.
He did not give the location of the ship, but Romania's interior ministry said it had sunk about 30 nautical miles south of its port of Sfantu Gheorghe.
"At around 11:00 (09:00 GMT), Coast Guard border police officers were informed that a fire had broken out on board a commercial vessel located within Romania's exclusive economic zone," the ministry said in a statement.
"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased persons have also been identified," it added.
Ukraine's president said he had "repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea" - and other countries had made "relevant proposals" too.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelensky said.
"Pressure is needed to restore global food security," he added. "And everyone who is genuinely interested in this must help."
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
President Vladimir Putin admitted last week Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP.
The Russian leader has also intensified his rhetoric against Western allies of Ukraine - repeating a threat of even using nuclear weapons.
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
The head of Germany's foreign intelligence Martin Jaeger said on Monday that "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia", which was "waging a shadow war" with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining "real and imminent".

A dead star’s wreckage may be the birthplace of a new planet.
The existence of second-generation planets was predicted theoretically more than 15 years ago. But this “phoenix” world, if confirmed, would be the first actually spotted, scientists report October 5 in Nature Astronomy.
“A phoenix is reborn from the ashes of its predecessor, and this planet is formed from the ashes of the star,” says astronomer Jamie Williams, of the University of Warwick in Coventry, England.
The finding suggests planetary systems can have a second life even after their stars die.
Before this discovery, this planet formation process has been “more like a hypothesis, more like speculation,” says planetary scientist Zifan Lin of Washington University in St. Louis, who was not involved in the new work. “This is the first time we’ve seen evidence for that process.”
Williams and colleagues found signs of the planet in the atmosphere of a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832. White dwarfs are the small, dense cores left behind after low-mass stars — like our sun — puff up into red giant stars at the end of their lives, ultimately blowing all the outer material away.
These stellar corpses are so dense that most chemical elements sink into their centers, leaving them with pristine atmospheres composed of almost entirely hydrogen and helium. But astronomers have found that between a quarter and half of these stars are “polluted” with elements like silicon and iron, which are found in rock.
These elements probably come from shattered planets that the star devoured as it expanded. “They can be probes into the interiors of planets,” Lin says. Astronomers have also found whole planets that seem to have survived their stars’ demise and still orbit the remaining white dwarf. Ironically, some astronomers think these dead stars could be prime hunting grounds for signs of extraterrestrial life.
HS 0209+0832 was a known weirdo. When the Hubble Space Telescope observed it in 1999, astronomers could tell that the white dwarf contained a mysterious mix of chemicals, but they couldn’t identify them. Since then, there have been more detailed studies of how certain atoms would show up in stellar atmospheres, Williams says.
Reanalyzing those observations showed that the white dwarf contains only trace amounts of silicon and almost no iron, Williams and colleagues found. But it does include a ridiculous amount of niobium. This hard, silvery metal, used in jewelry, rocket systems and superconductors, is rare on Earth and had never been seen in a white dwarf.
“We’ve never observed anything in the universe that’s this niobium-rich before,” Williams says. “We were quite confused at first.”
A clue to how it got there came from the element’s origins. Niobium forms in the slow neutron-capture process, or s-process, which mostly occurs in certain red giant stars as they shed their atmospheres and die. Iron nuclei transform into heavier elements in a series of accretion and decay that can take thousands of years.
Material ejected from a dying star could have coalesced into a new planet full of s-process elements, Williams says. Then the resulting white dwarf could slowly sip on the new planet’s atmosphere, leaving a fresh coat of niobium and other s-process elements on the white dwarf’s face.
To support this idea, the team looked at observations of HS 0209+0832 taken with the TESS space telescope, which hunts exoplanets by observing small changes in the light of their stars as planets orbit. The white dwarf’s brightness changes with a period of about 4.4 days, the team found. That’s too slow to be related to the white dwarf’s own rotation.
But it could be explained by a gas giant planet orbiting very close to the star, about 4 percent the distance from the Earth to the sun or 6 million kilometers. Williams imagines it as a silvery version of Jupiter.
“We’re not really sure, if it’s not a planet, what it is,” he says. “A planet is the most reasonable explanation.”
Our sun will one day meet the same fate as HS 0209+0832’s predecessor. We don’t know enough about second-generation planets yet to say whether our solar system could end up with one after the sun dies, Williams says. “But I think it’s definitely possible.”

US spy chief tapped as White House AI czar
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will now helm broad domestic technology and economic policy discussions.
The nation's top spy is now also the White House's AI czar.
President Donald Trump named Jay Clayton, who was sworn in as director of national intelligence in July, to lead what Trump referred to in a Truth Social post as the “Super Intelligence Force” meant to coordinate the government’s engagement with various organizations, critical-infrastructure providers, and AI companies.
Last month, Trump ordered federal agencies to start calling AI "super intelligence."
According to its charter, the task force will create plans to handle AI-enabled threats, streamline breach notifications, and improve government-response capacities while aiming to avoid overregulation. Its creation follows growing public concerns over AI safety and cybersecurity risks, as well as heated political discussions over the data-center buildouts that power many of today’s AI systems.
“The risk of not being first is high,” Clayton told the Wall Street Journal in a Saturday exclusive that discussed the task force. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries,” he said. “Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people.”
The task force has three vice chairs: Defense Undersecretary for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson. Its members include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and other senior advisors, alongside external advisors like venture capitalist David Sacks — who previously worked as Trump’s AI and crypto czar early in the administration — and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice. It will have 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of AI and establish a plan for the federal government to tackle it.
The panel’s establishment marks a shift for an administration that has predominantly maintained a hands-off approach toward AI governance. But officials have faced mounting pressure over the past six months to respond as a new generation of sophisticated, autonomous AI models demonstrating advanced cybersecurity capabilities have repeatedly circumvented or escaped technical safeguards.
Its creation highlights a steady group of voices in the administration and tech industry that believe the time for AI safeguard discussions should begin, though Trump and other officials have largely continued to lean toward a more relaxed approach to regulating the technology.
In public discussions, officials and researchers typically frame AI development as a trade-off between slowing down for safety and accelerating to maintain an edge over foreign adversaries pursuing AI for military and economic gains.
China has especially become a major player in the global AI race. Clayton’s appointment to the task force appears to signal a shift by the administration to cast AI as a geopolitical and national-security subject area.
His dual role is a unique move for the White House, placing the current DNI — who oversees the 18 U.S. spy agencies — at the helm of broad domestic technology and economic policy discussions. Clayton brings a background as a corporate lawyer and former SEC chairman, distinguishing him from tech-focused people from Silicon Valley.
AI has already transformed how spy agencies digest vast troves of collected data and build intelligence products, among other things.
Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that he welcomed the administration’s attention toward the fast-evolving technology but said Clayton’s new title lacks a coherent strategy.
“We still do not know what authority this new role will have, whether it will include developing safety standards or reviewing the most advanced models, or how it fits into the administration’s broader approach to AI,” Warner said in a statement. “That lack of clarity is especially concerning as leading AI companies themselves are confronting increasingly capable systems that can evade safeguards and exploit cybersecurity vulnerabilities.”
“I hope this appointment is an opportunity for the administration to move beyond slogans and toward a serious, coordinated national strategy for AI,” he said.

7c71207b2dfc.text: By — Mari Yamaguchi, Associated Press Mari Yamaguchi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-u-s-marine-has-been-arrested-in-the-killing-of-a-woman-on-okinawa-triggering-outrage-in-japan Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A U.S. Marine has been arrested in the killing of a woman on Okinawa, triggering outrage in Japan World Oct 5, 2026 10:50 AM EDT TOKYO (AP) — Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine accused of robbing and killing a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, in the latest criminal case involving U.S. military personnel on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence is a sensitive issue. READ MORE: Explosion at U.S. base on Okinawa injures 4 Japanese soldiers The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa's capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack early Saturday. Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman's body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled. Police said security camera footage showed a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Okinawa City's entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said. "The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged." "I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all," said Koja, referring to the U.S. military's measures taken in response to past criminal cases. Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan's southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands. Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan's central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military. "The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed "outrage," the ministry said in a statement. Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim's family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments. The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. "The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior." Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa's eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays. The rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members in 1995 sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrence of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
